title: "Did they get it all?"
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in general surgery. Mr Shah, 63, had a laparotomy yesterday for suspected bowel cancer. The surgeons found that the cancer had spread widely and couldn't be removed.

The consultant plans to talk to him this afternoon. When you see him this morning, he asks you, "Did they get it all?"
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Tell him the consultant will explain everything this afternoon.
options.detailed: The consultant should lead, but deflecting a direct question may leave him anxious for hours.

options.text: Reassure him that the operation went well.
options.detailed: The operation may have been technically uneventful, but implying it was successful would be dishonest.

options.text: Tell his wife first so she can be with him when he hears.
options.brief: He has capacity, and should hear about his own diagnosis first.
options.detailed: He may want his wife there, which you can offer, but telling her first, without his agreement, breaches his confidentiality.

options.text: Ask what he remembers being told so far.
options.brief: Helps you understand where he is starting from.
options.detailed: He may have been told something in recovery, or nothing. Finding out what he knows helps you respond appropriately.

options.text: Tell him gently and honestly that it couldn't be removed.
options.brief: He has asked directly, and is entitled to an honest answer.
options.detailed: If he wants to know, an honest, gentle answer respects him. You can explain that the consultant will discuss what it means and the options this afternoon.

options.text: Give him a leaflet about bowel cancer to read.
options.brief: Impersonal, and doesn't answer his question.
options.detailed: Written information can help later, but it isn't a substitute for a conversation.

options.text: Wait until he has recovered from surgery before discussing it.
options.brief: Delays news he has asked for.
options.detailed: He has asked now. Delaying may increase his anxiety and damage his trust.

options.text: Make sure the consultant knows he has asked.
options.brief: A fuller conversation should follow promptly.
options.detailed: The consultant can explain the findings and what comes next. Letting them know he is asking helps them prioritise seeing him.

explanation.issue: This tests how you answer a direct question about bad news when a senior plans a fuller discussion later.
explanation.keyDetails: He has asked directly. The cancer couldn't be removed. The consultant will see him this afternoon.
explanation.reasoning: [D] finds out what he knows, [E] answers honestly, and [H] makes sure the consultant follows up. The distractors deflect ([A], [G]), mislead ([B]), breach confidentiality ([C]), or are impersonal ([F]).
explanation.competing: [A] is tempting because the consultant should lead. But he has asked directly, and you can be honest while leaving the detail to the consultant.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 2, giving patients information honestly and sensitively.
